texts.wb-b6d606c4:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, where applicable, the
Environmental Information Regulations 2004, I request copies of records
relating to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, near Cardiff.

I am specifically seeking:

   1.

   Planning applications, permissions, refusals, conditions, appeals, and
   related correspondence concerning the demolition of Great House Farm and
   subsequent residential development.
   2.

   Any archaeological assessments, surveys, reports, briefs, watching
   briefs, excavation reports, or heritage impact assessments relating to the
   site.
   3.

   Any correspondence between the Council, Cadw, BP Properties, BP,
   developers, archaeologists, the Royal Commission, or other public bodies
   concerning:
   - Great House Farm;
      - its historic significance;
      - archaeological discoveries;
      - listing or scheduling considerations;
      - demolition proposals.
   4.

   Any records discussing reported Roman remains, medieval remains,
   monastic remains, burials, architectural fragments, or other archaeological
   features associated with the site.
   5.

   Any records relating to emergency listing, spot-listing, preservation,
   or protection measures considered for Great House Farm during the 1980s.
   6.

   Any committee minutes, officer reports, recommendations, or briefing
   papers relating to planning decisions affecting the site.

If some records are held in archives or under a different authority, please
advise where they may be located.

I would prefer the information in electronic format.

Yours faithfully,


Sion Buckler

https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz

Good afternoon,

Thank you very much for your enquiry. While we cannot advise you on a legal case or undertake a review of historical decisions, pleas note that we do hold information and archives related to Great House Farm, Llandough.

The site entry and description for the site in the National Monuments Record of Wales can be seen online on Coflein, here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182.

We hold 14 archives related to the site, a list of which can be seen here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182/archives?size=25. These archives can be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales, which is open Tuesday through Thursday, 9:30-16:30. If you would like to view the material in person, I would advise arranging with us beforehand so that we can prepare the material ahead of your visit. Some of the material is on microfiche and as we do not have a microfiche reader in the Search Room, we will need to liaise with the National Library Reading Room staff to try to negotiate the use of their machines ahead of your visit.

While it is possible to order scans of material using the attached order form, we may be unable to provide research-quality scans or photographs of some of the material, such as the material on microfiche, which would require high-resolution scanning at a cost of £20 per scan. Moreover,  many of these records remain under third-party copyright, and we would only be able to provide scans or copies for personal, non-commercial research. Other uses, such as use in a legal case or report would likely require the permission of the copyright holder(s). I would therefore advise arranging to view the material in person rather than ordering scans, if possible.

In addition to the information and records which we hold, there are several related records in the Historic Environment Record maintained by Heneb, which related to excavations, mostly concerning the cemetery/burial site:

  *   https://archwilio.org.uk/arch/query/page.php?watprn=GGAT03584s&dbname=ggat&tbname=core
  *   https://archwilio.org.uk/arch/query/page.php?watprn=GGAT03583s&dbname=ggat&tbname=core
  *   https://archwilio.org.uk/arch/query/page.php?watprn=GGAT03586s&dbname=ggat&tbname=core
  *   https://archwilio.org.uk/arch/query/page.php?watprn=GGAT03585s&dbname=ggat&tbname=core

Thank you very much again for your enquiry.

Sincerely,

Adam Coward

From: Requester <[redacted]>
Sent: 14 November 2025 12:49
To: kanishka.narayan.mp@parliament.uk
Subject: BP vs Buckler

You don't often get email from [redacted]<mailto:[redacted]>. Learn why this is important<https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification>

Sir/Ma'am,

I am your constituent, living [location redacted]. I am writing to request your assistance in reviewing a historic legal matter involving my family: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), relating to Great House Farm, Llandough.

My family lived on, cared for and claimed to own that farm for generations. The events surrounding the 1987 case resulted in the loss of our home and land, and left several members of my family deeply affected. Recent research I have undertaken has revealed significant procedural inconsistencies, historical irregularities, unanswered questions regarding corporate identity, unverified service of key documents, and heritage considerations relating to the site.

I have attached a short report summarising SOME of these issues. I am requesting your help in identifying the appropriate bodies-legal, historical, or governmental-who may be able to independently review the historical record to ensure fairness, accuracy, and transparency.

My interest is not solely personal; Great House Farm has a heritage significance to Wales, including documented accounts that Guglielmo Marconi stayed there while experimenting with early radio technology. I believe this should form part of our preserved historical record.

By way of background, I am a veteran and have served both in the Armed Forces and recently with the Vale of Glamorgan Council. My intention is simply to seek clarity, proper review, and justice where appropriate. I would be grateful for your guidance on the correct avenues to pursue.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler
[redacted]
Tel: 0203 137 7118
texts.wb-dfce78c8:
Good afternoon,

Thank you for your further enquiry. I have checked the accessions information for the archive items which we hold related to the site. Unfortunately, there is no accessions data for the items in the NMR Site File collection. This is because most of the information was either created (in the case of notes and drawing from site visits) or collected (in the case of the newspaper cuttings) by RCAHMW staff in the course of their duties. Having examined the records themselves, however, I do note that Archive Number 6048942 may have come from a Mrs Buckler (‘Mrs Buckler?’ is handwritten under the account). There is also a note at the bottom of Archive Number 6048945 that ‘Correspondence between C.N. Johns and Mrs Buckler, Great House Farm, has been lost since 1986/87’, although I have been unable to find any other record of this correspondence either in our records or our archive catalogue, having carried out both digital and physical searches, including searching through the RCAHMW administrative files in the archive (some of which are not yet open to the public).

With regard to the first three records in the list, I include what accessions details are available below:
Archive Number
creator or originating body

With regards to which records mention things like ownership and the dispute, most of the newspaper article clippings naturally discuss it. Archive Number 6048942 provides a short history of the site and notes the family’s residence there and Archive Number 6048945 notes that ‘The house remained partially recorded because of problems created by an ownership dispute. The house and farm buildings were suddenly and completely destroyed by B. P. Properties Ltd. on 6th December 1988 amid considerable local controversy’. If you would like further details about the content of these records, they can be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales, which is open Tuesday through Thursday. Scans of records can also be requested, using the attached order form. We also do offer a limited document summary service. Please see our price list for details.

In addition to these 14 records, we may hold some historical aerial photography which may include the site. Aelodau Anrhydeddus y Senedd,

Rwy’n ysgrifennu atoch i dynnu eich sylw at yr hyn yr wyf yn ei ystyried yn anghyfiawnder hanesyddol difrifol, yn ymwneud â’m teulu, y Bucklers, a dinistr Great House Farm yn Llandough — safle fferm a chartref o dros 800 mlynedd o hanes, gan gynnwys cysylltiadau mynachaidd a chysylltiad uniongyrchol â Guglielmo Marconi yn ystod datblygiad cynnar radio.

Mae’r mater hwn yn codi cwestiynau difrifol ynghylch hawliau tir, gweithdrefnau cyfreithiol, cofrestru tir, a hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Er enghraifft, mewn datganiad i’r wasg yn 1974, dywedodd fy nain yn gyhoeddus: “It’s my home.” Mae’r datganiad hwn, sydd yn fater o gofnod cyhoeddus, yn gwrth-ddweud yn uniongyrchol ganfyddiad Llys Apêl 1987 yn BP v Buckler, lle dywedwyd ei bod wedi bod yn “ddistaw” ac wedi derbyn trwydded BP a gyhoeddwyd yn 1974.

Yn yr un achos, gwrthodwyd apêl fy nhad ar y sail bod BP Pension Trust Ltd a BP Properties Ltd yn “effeithiol yr un cwmni”. Fodd bynnag, yn y dyfarniad yr oedd yn ei herio, nododd y barnwr nad oedd ymatebion fy nain i BP Pension Trust Ltd yn cyfrif gan mai BP Properties Ltd oedd yr hawlydd, ac mai cwmnïau ar wahân oeddent. Yn ymarferol, roedd hyn yn arwain at sefyllfa “pen y cwmni’n ennill, cynffon y teulu’n colli”.

Yn sgil hyn, cafodd fy nhad ei dynnu o’i wely ysbyty, ei garcharu heb gyhuddiad, a gosodwyd gorchymyn atal arno i’w atal rhag meddiannu ac amddiffyn ein fferm 800 oed rhag cael ei dymchwel. Cafodd ei gais i’r Llys Hawliau Dynol Ewropeaidd ei rwystro cyn iddo farw yn 1991, yn ddim ond 41 oed.

Ar y sail hon, rwy’n gofyn yn ffurfiol am Ddeiseb i sefydlu Ymchwiliad Cyhoeddus i’r achos hwn, fel mater o ddwyn tir hanesyddol ac o dorri hawliau dynol yng Nghymru.

Rwy’n weithiwr proffesiynol ym maes seiber a rhyfela electronig milwrol. Mae technolegau AI pwerus bellach ar gael i bob un ohonom, ac nid oes unrhyw reswm technegol pam na ellid archwilio’r mater hwn yn llawn ac yn drylwyr. Mae’r hyn a ddigwyddodd i’m teulu yn ymddangos fel anghyfiawnder dwys, aml-genhedlaethol, ac yn debyg i ffurf ar “lawfare”, lle y trinwyd fy nheulu fel llafur di-dâl i gynnal ased tir hyd nes yr oedd yn gyfleus i’w ariannu. Ceir honiadau bod sylw sylweddol yn y wasg yn 1974 o blaid fy nain a’n teulu, ynghyd â deiseb o tua 1,700 o bobl yn ceisio atal dymchwel y fferm. Ymhellach, mae’n ymddangos bod CADW wedi methu ag ymyrryd lle dylai’r safle fod wedi cael statws Adeilad Rhestredig Gradd II.

Nid wyf yn sicr a gofnodwyd erioed yn briodol yn y Gofrestrfa Tir fod y tir — a gofrestrwyd gan BP yn 1982 — dan anghydfod. Yn fy nealltwriaeth i, cafodd ei drin fel pe na bai mewn anghydfod o gwbl. Roedd mam Marconi hefyd yn Jamerson o gwmni wisgi Gwyddelig Jameson. Rwy’n gofyn i chi gynnal eich ymchwil eich hun, gwneud eich ymholiadau eich hun, a dod i’ch casgliadau eich hun — ond yn anad dim, peidiwch â chaniatáu i hanes gael ei ailysgrifennu yma.

Mae fy nheulu bellach yn archwilio opsiynau ar gyfer siarad cyhoeddus, hawliau stori, a dogfennaeth. Yn nhermau cysylltiadau teuluol: fy nhaid oedd Ray Smith o Dempsey and Makepeace; mae fy modryb yn Shan Cothi; a dechreuodd fy ewythr y band Tigertailz.

Rwy’n disgrifio’r sefyllfa hon fel gwarthus. Mae fy ngwraig a minnau’n amharod i ganiatáu i’n merch hyd yn oed gamu ar Ynysoedd Prydain o ystyried yr hyn a glywn sy’n digwydd yno. Yn 2024, allforiais hyd yn oed fy nghi o Abertawe i’n heiddo yn y Caribî ar ôl i unigolyn Afghanistan fod yng ngardd fy nheulu yng Nghymru, gan geisio ei ddwyn.

Dear Mr. Gale,

Thank you again for your helpful reply and for viewing the original
Manorial Documents Committee returns (HMC9/311). I entirely understand that
it is difficult to advise further without more specifics, and I am grateful
for the steer toward the Penrice and Margam Estate Records and the NLW
catalogue.

To answer your question directly: the document historically referred to
within the family as the *“Williams Title”* (or the equitable interest
conveyance that underpinned it) dates to the period *c. 1900–1915*. It
arises from an agreement between John Williams (occupier of Great House
Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin) and Daniel Thomas & Son (Bute Estate quarry
operators / limestoners). In essence, the Williams family granted
permission for quarrying on part of the farm in return for equitable title
/ permanent security of tenure once quarrying was complete. Daniel Thomas
is said to have formalised his side by a land-swap deed with the Bute
Estate (copy formerly held in Cardiff Library, now reported missing along
with its index card in 1984).

This places the key transaction squarely in the early 20th-century Bute
estate rationalisation period, immediately before the 1916 agricultural
tenancy to John Williams and the 1915 death of Daniel Thomas (after which
Bute attempted eviction, only for the equitable interest to be asserted
successfully at the time). Family testimony, supported by the 1876
limeworks severance (Glamorgan Archives D153/4-8) and the known industrial
quarrying context, points to this narrow window as the origin of the modern
title dispute.

*Why this matters now* The 1987 Court of Appeal decision (*BP Properties
Ltd v Buckler*) turned on the technical effect of 1974 unilateral licence
letters addressed to “Mrs Buckler” – a name my grandmother Mary Williams
(née Williams) never used in her marriage or death records. By addressing
her under this legal fiction, the proceedings bypassed any adjudication of
the Williams equitable title that had been recognised as late as 1915. As
the principle “fraud unravels all” makes clear, once the foundational
misnomer is identified, the entire chain of subsequent possession orders,
licences and registration falls to be re-examined. My grandmother and her
heirs therefore retain the superior land claim; the 1988 dispossession and
demolition of the 800-year-old farmhouse constitute actionable loss for
which reparations are now sought.

To strengthen the evidential base I have prepared a one-page interactive
timeline (hosted at [insert your hosted link here after uploading]) that
highlights every event directly relevant to the “Williams Title” period.
With your elevated archival access, you will immediately see where to focus
searches in the Penrice and Margam or Bute collections (e.g., 1895–1916
leases, conveyances, limeworks/quarrying files, and any Daniel Thomas
references).

I would be most grateful if you could now guide me to the precise
sub-series or box references within those collections that cover Llandough
manorial transactions in the 1900–1916 window. Any surviving index cards,
rental entries, or correspondence mentioning John Williams / Daniel Thomas
in connection with Great House Farm would be transformative.

Thank you once more for your time and expertise. I look forward to your
further assistance.

Kind regards

Sion Buckler

> FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR
> ENGAGEMENT
>
>
>
> Dear Sir/Madam,
>
>
>
> This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance.
> It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence,
> deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice
> constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to
> be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process,
> and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and
> discrepancies identified.
>
>
>
> This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage;
> formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our
> family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history
> rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry,
> archaeology, and public records.
>
>
>
> My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William
> Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v
> Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose
> dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination
> remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and
> materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records
> as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and
> which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings.
> The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired
> and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family
> records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.
>
>
>
> I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak
> publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain
> too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these
> proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of
> livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession.
> That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment
> of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence
> produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.
>
>
>
> The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational
> pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100
> granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through
> monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial
> encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern
> corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an
> 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless
> and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological
> vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and
> medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier
> discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet
> heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.
>
>
>
> The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They
> have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:
>
>
>
> 1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of
> Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection
> arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until
> our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
>
> 2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as
> executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and
> matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record,
> restitution, and restorative remedies.
>
>
>
> These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record
> pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through
> procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.
>
>
>
> In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and
> obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims
> grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined
> inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus
> domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere
> occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not
> ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were
> adjourned or quashed without resolution.
>
>
>
> This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:
>
>
>
> *       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938
> auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
>
> *       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo
> Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased
> from records).
>
> *       Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying
> permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.
>
>
>
> Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage
> protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising
> credibility concerns.
>
>
>
> Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not
> right with the record:
>
>
>
> *       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4
> November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
>
> *       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny
> unsupported by verifiable coverage.
>
> *       Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title
> determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
>
> *       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family
> detriment.
>
> *       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g.,
> interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings
> dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
>
> *       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches
> ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid
> development).
>
> *       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert
> Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).
>
> *       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough
> Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of
> the "battleground" site.
>
>
>
> These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation
> (e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales'
> cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is
> illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and
> moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but
> passage of time does not validate it.
>
>
>
> Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment
> (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for
> reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.
>
>
>
> I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders
> (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs,
> historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively,
> review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further
> rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable
> evidence available.
>
>
>
> This Notice:
>
>
>
> *       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
>
> *       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
>
> *       Reserves all rights without prejudice.
>
> *       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may
> aggravate responsibility.
>
>
>
> For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.
>
>
>
> This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance
> becomes untenable.
>
>
>
> Regards, Requester On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [redacted],
> [location redacted], Vale of Glamorgan, Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/ <
> https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/>
>
>
>
> Postscript — Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The
> heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a
> young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or
> differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality
> Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability
> cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of
> ignorance.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to formally report a long-standing and systemic case of what I suspect may be dispossession, fraudulent misrepresentation, and archaeological suppression concerning my family’s ancestral land, Great House Farm (historically Tŷ Mawr/Cedfin), Llandough.

I am the descendant of the Williams/Buckler family, who held de facto possession and indigenous tenure of this land from 1667 until our forced displacement in 1988. I am currently the only member of my family who is not too traumatized to speak of these events. My mother (Mary Williams daughter in law), remains to this day too terrified to speak up about this multi-generational "lawfare" campaign waged against us. Our family have not seen justice or received reperations, nor have we sued or reopened this case under limitations act clauses of fraud and consealment. Yet. But this may not be just a grave injustice upon our family, but our nations archeological history and indigenous people on our ancestral birthland. We are Welsh Nationals, Welsh speaking, under Welsh flags. This is some British Colonisation-grade trespass I'm seeing and it's tandamount to a declaration of civil war on me, my family, community and people.

The core of this report involves the following suspicions I have of concealment and fraud (see attached for my timeline and notes):

  1.  Archaeological Suppression: In 1888, my family discovered a Roman soldier in full armor beneath the living room floorboards. This discovery provided "actual notice" of the site's national significance a century before its demolition. We allege this notice was systematically suppressed by corporate and state actors to allow for commercial development.

  2.  Fraudulent Misrepresentation in Planning: During the 1987 planning process, the 13th-century fortified manor was described by developers as a "dilapidated utility building" or "ruined barn" to secure a demolition permit that would have otherwise been denied under heritage protection laws.

  3.  Legal Identity Falsification: In 1974, BP Pension Trust issued a "unilateral license" intended to bypass our possessory title. This correspondence was falsely addressed to "Mrs. Buckler" to bind my grandmother to her deceased husband’s name and legal status, despite her public rejection of their claim. She used her maiden name Williams and her husband Bucklers' intent to accept license died with him. My nan also alledgedly didn't expressly deny the offer and so accepted through her silence. But she was near enough voiceless from screaming for decades that she will not do deals with any of them. That's a different kind of silence, if any. And to have responded to license to Mrs Buckler would have been identify fraud as she was Mrs Williams. And she did in fact reject BPs license offer and advanced, countless times, but publically. I believe these objections were suppressed too. There's allegedly news coverage from October 30th 1974 but I'm yet to find the evidence. But see attached a 1978 article I unearthed. My nan clearly maintains her position "It's my home".   [cid:ii_19c31438f12e2e321bc2]

  4.  You'll also see in landmark legal case BP Vs Buckler 1987 the judge says that she might have responded to BP, but to BP Pension Trust, but the claimant was BP Properties Ltd which were two separate companies. But in my dads appeal when he challenges that BP Pension Trust Ltd should have been the claimant the same judge dismissed his appeal citing both BP companies are effectively the same. This is clearly a case of heads BP won, Tails we lost.

  5.  Missing Evidence: Critical title deeds and Bute Estate records from our families deal with Daniel Thomas, for title after quarrying completed, in exchange for our permission to quarry, also disappeared from the loft of our home and the Cardiff Library according to my families accounts, precisely when they were needed to support our ownership claim in the Court of Appeal. Regardless we should have still remained on grounds we'd been there since 1667, and failing that on grounds of adverse possession.

  6.  It was evident lawfare to remove us, to get to the burials known about since 1888, BP profited from the land sale, the state and Crown have the exhevated artifacts and my displaced family are left traumatised, cheated and dead. My dad's appeal was dismissed to when it shouldn't have been and his ECHR request blocked, before dying abruptly at age just 41.

The confirmation in 1994 of a high-status Roman villa and over 1,000 burials on the exact site of our demolished home proves that the "official narrative" used to evict us was predicated on the concealment of known facts.

Under Section 32 of the Limitation Act 1980, the limitation period for action does not begin until such fraud or concealment is discovered. As the heir to this possessory title, I am seeking a formal investigation into the institutional failures that permitted this dispossession and the destruction of a national monument.

I have compiled my account and understanding of these events in timeline order and I'm prepared to provide further testimony and evidence.

Given the extreme trauma my family has suffered, I request that all correspondence be handled with the gravity this human rights violation deserves.

Considering the lack of cooperation from my traumatised family. And authorities who maybe complicit and implicated. And possible corruption of records and fraud and consealment, I'm open to the fact my account and understanding may not be perfect. But if even a single other person or group looked into this too, even briefly, I'm sure you'll agree there's merrit to the concerns I'm raising with all of this.

I look forward to your response regarding the appropriate next steps for investigation and restitution.

I do ask for some small sense of urgency in that justice delayed is justice denied. I understand this is ancient news for many, but my family still feel a tremendous sense of disposition and disposition over all of this. Bringing this all up means to re live it.

I will have been 3 or 4 at the time, but I still remember my toys in our house, being bulldozed. And my mum handing us rocks to throw at them, bulldozing down our home. As my dad was held without charges to prevent him defending us and our home. I'd have to visit him in a hospital bed after his heart attack and see him in a coffin shortly afterwards.

I'm 41 years old now. I'm a certified and experienced military commander and leader. I left my military career with honours. I finished 22 years in Oath in 2024, bond afide, my last 2 employed under the Welsh government.

I kindly request but also require of you, that this matter be layed to rest correctly.

My family never surrendered. Never relinquished claim to that land. We we're in honour in that we weren't there with force, stealth/ secrecy or license. But BP and the British State did use force, stealth/ secrecy and license.

All things considered I believe I find myself in honour here, and the British Establishment in dishonour. This matter must be escalated. I'm duty bound.


Regards,


Sion Buckler

Dear Requester,

Thank you for your email regarding Great House Farm, Llandough. However, I must inform you that much of the content in your correspondence falls outside the scope of Cadw’s work.

In relation to the claim of 'archaeological suppression' involving the discovery of a Roman soldier in full armour in 1888, any such find would typically have been reported in the antiquarian press at either the national or local level. It is possible that records of this nature may be held by local museums. It is worth noting that the first Ancient Monuments Act was passed in 1882, focusing solely on bringing threatened ancient monuments into guardianship. The legal recognition of nationally important archaeology did not come about until the Ancient Monuments Consolidation and Amendment Act of 1913.

Upon reviewing the Cof Cymru database, I found that there are no designated historic assets relevant to this topic. However, Archwilio contains two records that document the involvement of the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT):

1. Great House Farm HER site entry - GGAT03586s
2. Land at Great House Farm HER event entry - GGATE003872, which includes GGAT's 1990 archaeological assessment report commissioned by BP Properties Ltd.

Any advice or correspondence that Cadw may have provided should be preserved in the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW) National Monuments Record of Wales (NMRW). I recommend you contact the NMRW to access any relevant documents. Additionally, you may want to reach out to Heneb and the Vale of Glamorgan Local Planning Authority (LPA) to explore what records they might hold concerning this matter.

Kind regards,

Jenna Arnold

Hi Requester,

Thank you for your detailed follow-up and for sharing more about your
background and the historical context surrounding Great House Farm. I can
see how deeply this case matters to you and your family, and it’s clear
that you’ve invested considerable time and research into gathering evidence
and preserving your family’s story.

While developments in AI and digital archives have certainly made it easier
to uncover historic material and cross-reference records, the legal
framework for reopening a judgment remains essentially unchanged. Courts
still apply the same very strict criteria under CPR 52.30 and the
Limitation Act 1980, and they would require evidence of fraud, deliberate
concealment, or procedural impropriety at the time of the original
proceedings — not just new access to historical material or
reinterpretation through technology.

Even with emerging evidence, after nearly forty years the doctrine of
finality in litigation makes it exceptionally difficult to revisit property
cases that have long been settled. The courts are unlikely to reopen such a
matter unless the new evidence conclusively proves that the original
judgment was obtained through deception or corruption.

That said, the historical and human side of your family’s story — including
the Marconi connection and the loss of the farm — is genuinely fascinating.
It may have cultural or documentary value even if it has no remaining legal
remedy. If you do decide to pursue a documentary or historical feature, I’d
be happy to keep in touch and follow any developments from a reporting
standpoint.

Thank you again for writing, and I wish you every success in your efforts
to document and preserve this important piece of Welsh history.

Best regards,
Tom Sinclair

> FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR
> ENGAGEMENT
>
>
>
> Dear Sir/Madam,
>
>
>
> This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance.
> It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence,
> deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice
> constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to
> be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process,
> and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and
> discrepancies identified.
>
>
>
> This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage;
> formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our
> family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history
> rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry,
> archaeology, and public records.
>
>
>
> My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William
> Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v
> Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose
> dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination
> remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and
> materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records
> as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and
> which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings.
> The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired
> and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family
> records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.
>
>
>
> I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak
> publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain
> too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these
> proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of
> livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession.
> That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment
> of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence
> produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.
>
>
>
> The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational
> pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100
> granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through
> monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial
> encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern
> corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an
> 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless
> and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological
> vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and
> medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier
> discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet
> heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.
>
>
>
> The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They
> have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:
>
>
>
> 1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of
> Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection
> arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until
> our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
>
> 2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as
> executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and
> matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record,
> restitution, and restorative remedies.
>
>
>
> These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record
> pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through
> procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.
>
>
>
> In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and
> obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims
> grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined
> inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus
> domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere
> occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not
> ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were
> adjourned or quashed without resolution.
>
>
>
> This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:
>
>
>
> *       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938
> auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
>
> *       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo
> Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased
> from records).
>
> *       Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying
> permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.
>
>
>
> Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage
> protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising
> credibility concerns.
>
>
>
> Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not
> right with the record:
>
>
>
> *       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4
> November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
>
> *       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny
> unsupported by verifiable coverage.
>
> *       Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title
> determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
>
> *       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family
> detriment.
>
> *       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g.,
> interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings
> dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
>
> *       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches
> ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid
> development).
>
> *       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert
> Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).
>
> *       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough
> Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of
> the "battleground" site.
>
>
>
> These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation
> (e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales'
> cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is
> illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and
> moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but
> passage of time does not validate it.
>
>
>
> Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment
> (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for
> reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.
>
>
>
> I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders
> (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs,
> historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively,
> review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further
> rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable
> evidence available.
>
>
>
> This Notice:
>
>
>
> *       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
>
> *       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
>
> *       Reserves all rights without prejudice.
>
> *       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may
> aggravate responsibility.
>
>
>
> For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.
>
>
>
> This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance
> becomes untenable.
>
>
>
> Regards, Requester On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [redacted],
> [location redacted], Vale of Glamorgan, Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/ <
> https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/>
>
>
>
> Postscript — Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The
> heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a
> young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or
> differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality

In order to proceed with your request we require some further information:


  *   Please provide the title number in which you require this information for

You may need to apply for a Search of the Index Map to find out if a specific property or area of land is registered and, if it is, the title number(s) of that land. Further information on this service is provided below.

Once you have sufficiently clarified the relevant land in which you would like this information for, we will proceed with your request.

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware the information you have requested is held within our registers that are open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we are unable to provide access to this information via an Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) or a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request and it is likely a refusal notice will be issued for this information.

Information about how to apply to inspect or obtain official copies is contained with practice guide 11:
www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Our Customer Support colleagues are trained to handle queries which relate to information that is held on the register of title
If you require any assistance in completing the application form or to determine which documents to order, please contact our Customer Support Team who will be able to assist you with your query.

Their contact details are as follows:

English language phone 0300 006 0411
Welsh language phone 0300 006 0422

Telephone lines are open between 08:00 and 17:00 Monday to Friday This does not include Bank Holidays.
Website: www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>

What is the Index Map?
HM Land Registry keeps a computerised 'index map' based on the Ordnance Survey map. This computerised map provides an index of the land in every registered title and pending application for first registration.

Applying for an Index Map Search
You apply for an official search of the index map using form SIM<https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/index-map-application-for-an-official-search-sim>.
This will need to be printed, completed and sent to our Standard address<https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-address-for-applications#standard-addresses>.
You must attach a plan to show the land that you are interested in, it should:


  *        be drawn to scale
  *        be based on the current large scale Ordnance Survey map
  *        indicate scale and north point
  *        show property extent with suitable colouring and position in relation to nearby roads and other features plans of flats and maisonettes
     indicate floor level (if any) of the property.
  *
You can also search by map on our Search for land and property information<https://www.gov.uk/search-property-information-land-registry> service.

I found a lot of fraud & concealment in this case. There's also a lot of media coverage in archives. I wondered if the clause in the limitations act could allow me to reopen the case on these grounds. The museum confirmed to be last week all the items exhevated from under our farm after it was stolen from us.

I'll give you one of the 12 arguments I have where it concerns clauses in the limitation act to reopen the case. My nan fought off the alleged possessor, BP Pensions Trust Ltd, for many years - and  maintained equitable title ownership of our 800 year old farm. But the judge ruled that BP Properties Ltd, the claimant in the 1987 case, were ignored. And the BP companies were seperate, so rejecting one doesn't inherently meaning rejecting the other. And so their letter of offer, a license to stay at "their" farm until she died, upheld and stopped the clock on adverse possession. Which was the position of our family (since our title deeds had gone missing from our home and copy gone from the public library during all this multi generational lawfare).

But in my dads appeal (point 3/3) he argued BP Pensions Trust should have been the claimant, not BP Properties Ltd. To which the judges dismissed the appeal citing - both BP companies are basically the same.

So a blatant case of "Heads they win, tails we lose". Not to mention the relationship between British Government and BP in those years being a huge bias.

Furthermore my nan wasn't alive to defend her position in 87. And no evidence was presented of the alleged letter from BP to stop the clock of adverse possession. Yet the case was won on the fact a letter of rejection, from a now dead woman, wasn't able to be presented. It is insane how BP took possession of our family farm of 400 years of occupancy.

Our farm was prime real estate, overlooking Cardiff bay. This is an Erin Brokovitch scale scandal. It gets more wild. In my research I discovered Marconi stayed with us while inventing Radio. My great grandad took him via horse & cart every day, to Lavenock Point Penarth, to conduct his radio experiments - including the day of the first successful broadcast. There's not even a plaque there today to commemorate that Llandough is the birthplace of radio. I'm also a decorated Royal Signals veteran (honourable discharge). Just 23 houses built over the site now. CADW expressly rejected a petition at the time too, which would afford our 800 year old farm protection from demolishment. Not only was the farm demolished, it was done during the night and early morning after the lawfare in the court which is an evident act of  desperation and relentlessness.

My family would like justice. I believe we have a strong case. The councillor of Llandough is very interested. I just need legal representation to take this forward.

I look forward to your reply on that matter too if you wouldn't mind. I did call and leave a message about it last week as well.


Regards,

If you are concerned about the condition of a historic site or ancient monument please contact the Welsh Government’s Historic Environment Service, Cadw or the relevant local authority. The Royal Commission’s primary role is to create, curate and communicate information on the historic environment, we also play a role as consultees in the planning process for the historic environment on the basis of this information. Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your e-mail and additional information explaining the background to your enquiry.

Unfortunately, apart from the pre-war survey returns The National Archives has only the only information recorded on-line MDR, and the following entry appears most pertinent to your enquiry held at the Glamorgan Archives: court book, with other manors D/D B M/3<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/N14274780> for 1884-1937 held at Glamorgan Archives. We do not hold any other finding manorial finding aids such as old index cards as the entries were updated in 1990’s summarising the archive services catalogues of the time. Also, I have no more access or information relating to the various archive collections held outside of The National Archives than any other researcher. The Bute Estate Archives held at the Glamorgan Archive Service are catalogued under collection reference DB: Bute, Glamorgan Estate<https://canfod.glamarchives.gov.uk/en/records/DB>

The only physical source we hold is a paper copy of the catalogue of 370 pages of the ‘Stuart family, Marquesses of Bute Archives: manorial records and estate papers, mainly rel to Glamorgan and Monmouthshire estates’ deposited at the National Library of Wales (NLW) in July 1950 (Ref. NRA 581) which submitted to the National of Register of Archives which now has a summarised entry in our on-line catalogue Discovery: Glamorganshire (Cardiff, Llantrisant, etc) and Monmouthshire (Newport, Machen, etc, NRA Stuart 581<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/N13577100> The reference to the Manors of Leckwith, Llandough, Cogan Cosmeston and Walterson is M17, pages 113-116 of the catalogue although most of the material predates 1900. This can be viewed at the library reading room at The National Archive by prior appointment. The Bute Estate archives for Glamorgan appear to be held at the National Library of Wales and the Glamorgan Archive Service. The NLW paper catalogue (Ref. NRA 581) broadly mirrors the NLW on-line catalogue: Bute Estate Records, - National Library of Wales Archives and Manuscripts<https://archives.library.wales/index.php/bute-estate-records>

A possibility worth bearing in mind is that the property, Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin may ceased to have been held by copyhold tenure by 1900 and instead may have been held instead by a leasehold tenancy which if this was the case the manorial records will not be relevant to your research. As you mentioned the Bute estate interests were steadily disposed of from c1900 culminating in sale of the estate’s leasehold interest to the Western Ground Rents Company in 1938. This led to the widespread dispersal and possibly destruction of the Bute estate records which makes it particularly challenging to track down and identify individual documents. Furthermore, catalogues often include bundle lists with individual documents concealed by a general description of the contents of the whole bundle.

I regret I cannot be of any further assistance; however I hope your further research proves fruitful.

Kind regards

I entirely understand that it is difficult to advise further without more specifics, and I am grateful for the steer toward the Penrice and Margam Estate Records and the NLW catalogue.

To answer your question directly: the document historically referred to within the family as the “Williams Title” (or the equitable interest conveyance that underpinned it) dates to the period c. 1900–1915. It arises from an agreement between John Williams (occupier of Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin) and Daniel Thomas & Son (Bute Estate quarry operators / limestoners). In essence, the Williams family granted permission for quarrying on part of the farm in return for equitable title / permanent security of tenure once quarrying was complete. Daniel Thomas is said to have formalised his side by a land-swap deed with the Bute Estate (copy formerly held in Cardiff Library, now reported missing along with its index card in 1984).

This places the key transaction squarely in the early 20th-century Bute estate rationalisation period, immediately before the 1916 agricultural tenancy to John Williams and the 1915 death of Daniel Thomas (after which Bute attempted eviction, only for the equitable interest to be asserted successfully at the time). Family testimony, supported by the 1876 limeworks severance (Glamorgan Archives D153/4-8) and the known industrial quarrying context, points to this narrow window as the origin of the modern title dispute.

Why this matters now The 1987 Court of Appeal decision (BP Properties Ltd v Buckler) turned on the technical effect of 1974 unilateral licence letters addressed to “Mrs Buckler” – a name my grandmother Mary Williams (née Williams) never used in her marriage or death records. By addressing her under this legal fiction, the proceedings bypassed any adjudication of the Williams equitable title that had been recognised as late as 1915. As the principle “fraud unravels all” makes clear, once the foundational misnomer is identified, the entire chain of subsequent possession orders, licences and registration falls to be re-examined. My grandmother and her heirs therefore retain the superior land claim; the 1988 dispossession and demolition of the 800-year-old farmhouse constitute actionable loss for which reparations are now sought.

To strengthen the evidential base I have prepared a one-page interactive timeline (hosted at [insert your hosted link here after uploading]) that highlights every event directly relevant to the “Williams Title” period. With your elevated archival access, you will immediately see where to focus searches in the Penrice and Margam or Bute collections (e.g., 1895–1916 leases, conveyances, limeworks/quarrying files, and any Daniel Thomas references).

I would be most grateful if you could now guide me to the precise sub-series or box references within those collections that cover Llandough manorial transactions in the 1900–1916 window. Any surviving index cards, rental entries, or correspondence mentioning John Williams / Daniel Thomas in connection with Great House Farm would be transformative.

Thank you once more for your time and expertise. I look forward to your further assistance.

Kind regards

Sion Buckler

  2.  Indexed in some manner (e.g., an index card or catalogue reference) that persisted even after the original document could not be located.

My understanding of the MDR — as described on your own website — is that it exists to provide brief descriptions of manorial records and details of their locations:

“An official index of English and Welsh manorial records providing brief descriptions of documents and details of their locations… It does not include title deeds or conveyances, and is not a register of ownership of manorial lordships or rights.”
https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

Based on that description, I would be grateful if you could confirm whether:

  1.  Any catalogue entries, index cards, reference pointers, or archival descriptions relating to the Manor of Llandough or the Williams family title exist in the MDR or related archival catalogues.
  2.  If so, the reference identifiers and information on how these can be consulted in person or via digitised records.

To be precise, I am looking for historical references to the index card or listing for the Williams Title — whether held in a library, local record office, or other institutional archive — rather than a claim for ownership judgment itself.

If such a reference does not currently appear in the MDR, I would greatly appreciate guidance on where any known catalogue cards or entry lists for manorial documents from Glamorgan / Llandough prior to 1950 might now reside (e.g., regional archives, National Archives holdings, or affiliated local repository catalogues).

Anyway I anticipate your forgiveness, if I have erred in writing to you earlier.

Thank you again and in advance for your assistance.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR ENGAGEMENT



Dear Sir/Madam,



This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence, deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process, and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and discrepancies identified.



This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.



My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.



I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.



The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.



The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:



1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.

2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.



These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.



In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.



This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:



*       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).

*       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).

*       Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.



Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising credibility concerns.



Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:



*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.

*       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.

*       Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.

*       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.

*       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).

*       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).

*       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).

*       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.



These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but passage of time does not validate it.



Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.



I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs, historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively, review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable evidence available.



This Notice:



*       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.

*       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.

*       Reserves all rights without prejudice.

*       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.



For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.



This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance becomes untenable.



Regards, Requester On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [address redacted], Vale of Glamorgan, Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/ <https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/>



Postscript — Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of ignorance.

Dear Mr Gale,

Thank you for your reply of 12 February. I would like to clarify and narrow
my request to ensure there is no misunderstanding regarding the records I
am trying to locate.

My correspondence is *not* seeking an adjudication of ownership or title —
I fully accept the stated remit boundaries of the Manorial Documents
Register (MDR). Rather, my enquiry concerns the existence of *any archival
reference, index card, catalogue entry, or pointer to a document
historically known as the “Williams Title”*, which was, according to
contemporaneous family testimony, at one point:

   1.

   Held in the *local public library* in the first half of the twentieth
   century; and
   2.

   Indexed in some manner (e.g., an index card or catalogue reference) that
   persisted even after the original document could not be located.

My understanding of the MDR — as described on your own website — is that it
exists to provide brief descriptions of manorial records and details of
their locations:

“An official index of English and Welsh manorial records providing brief
descriptions of documents and details of their locations… It does *not*
include title deeds or conveyances, and is *not* a register of ownership of
manorial lordships or rights.”
https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search
<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

Based on that description, I would be grateful if you could confirm whether:

   1.

   *Any catalogue entries, index cards, reference pointers, or archival
   descriptions* relating to the *Manor of Llandough* or the *Williams
   family title* exist in the MDR or related archival catalogues.
   2.

   If so, the *reference identifiers* and information on how these can be
   consulted in person or via digitised records.

To be precise, I am looking for historical references to the *index card or
listing* for the Williams Title — whether held in a library, local record
office, or other institutional archive — rather than a claim for ownership
judgment itself.

If such a reference does not currently appear in the MDR, I would greatly
appreciate guidance on where any known catalogue cards or entry lists for
manorial documents from *Glamorgan / Llandough* prior to 1950 might now
reside (e.g., regional archives, National Archives holdings, or affiliated
local repository catalogues).

Anyway I anticipate your forgiveness, if I have erred in writing to you
earlier.

Thank you again and in advance for your assistance.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler

Royal Commission,

I am researching the demolition of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth, in December 1988 (HER reference GGAT02038s / ST 1681 7331).

I am seeking to establish whether the Royal Commission was consulted or notified before the farmhouse was demolished.

Contemporary reports from 3 December 1988 state that Cadw was considering emergency protection/listing of Great House Farm and that a Cadw inspection was being arranged, including discussion with the Royal Commission for Ancient and Historical Monuments.

The farmhouse was then demolished on 6 December 1988.

I understand that the statutory framework at the time included provisions concerning the recording of historic buildings before authorised demolition. I would therefore be grateful if you could check your records and confirm:

  1.  Whether the Royal Commission received any notification, consultation, referral or request for advice concerning Great House Farm before its demolition in December 1988.
  2.  Whether the Royal Commission was asked to inspect, photograph, record or otherwise document the building before demolition.
  3.  Whether any correspondence exists between the Royal Commission, Cadw, the local planning authority, BP Properties Ltd, or their representatives concerning the proposed demolition.
  4.  Whether the Royal Commission was given an opportunity to complete or supplement its earlier recording of the farmhouse before demolition.
  5.  Whether your records contain any photographs, measured drawings, reports, field notes or other documentation relating specifically to the farmhouse immediately before its demolition.
  6.  If records exist, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers and, where possible, copies.

For context, the Royal Commission had already recorded Great House Farm architecturally in 1974. Contemporary material indicates that the building was subsequently under consideration for emergency listing shortly before its destruction.

There is also an important chronology concerning the occupation and possession of the property: my late father William Buckler had lodged European Commission of Human Rights application 14464/88 on 3 May 1988; BP obtained possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and the Strasbourg application was registered on 12 December 1988.

I am not asking the Royal Commission to express an opinion on the ownership dispute or the legality of the demolition. I am simply seeking to establish, from your records, whether the Commission was notified or consulted and what opportunity, if any, it was given to record the building (our home since 1667) before it was destroyed?

Given the historical and archaeological significance subsequently identified at the site, I would particularly appreciate confirmation of whether any pre-demolition recording was requested or undertaken.

Regards
[cid:image001.jpg@01DD468C.C3547200]

,



Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Sirs/ Ma'ams,

I need to correct a date I have used in earlier correspondence about Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, titles WA231076 and WA240304.

I had treated 1983 as the year the two titles were merged. That was wrong. HM Land Registry’s own letter of 23 March 2026 (Lisa Griffiths, ref N610CGV) separates the two acts.
1982–83 was first registration of two live titles, not a merger.
30 November 1982: application to first-register WA231076. The Court of Appeal later treated BP Properties Ltd as registered proprietors of “the farm” from November 1982.
23 February 1983: application to first-register a second title, WA240304.
26 March 1983: Mary Williams died. On the family’s case, notice of those applications did not reach us until after her death, while the family was in mourning. She had no window in which to object. The family was not in a position to use any window that arrived after that.
Those two titles remained separate through first instance.
24 July 1986: Hollis J. Both titles were still live. The judgment language treats Great House Farm as one holding. It had not been one holding on the register. On the family’s case it had not been one holding since the 1877 split: Parcel A (house, buildings, garden/yard and about 10 acres, the Thomas/Williams line) and Parcel B (the eastern fields retained by Bute and later WGR/BP).
2 February 1987: application to amalgamate the two titles. WA240304 was then closed and registration continued under WA231076. That is the merge. It was made after the 1986 ruling and before the Court of Appeal gave judgment on 31 July 1987.
So 1983 is silent first registration of a second title while Mary was still in Parcel A, or had only just died. 1987 is the administrative merger, carried out while the appeal was still open.
This was not a dispute about a single land parcel that BP already owned. Mary was on Parcel A, which the family says she owned, with occupation on that house parcel running in the family from at least 1667. BP, and WGR before it from 1949, were the neighbouring interest on Parcel B. From 1949 onwards the family’s case is that those neighbours ran a decades-long series of tenancy offers, “whole farm” wording, possession orders and the 1974 letters to make her occupation of her own parcel look permissive, and to make both parcels look like one estate they had acquired. They never produced a conveyance of Parcel A. What they had was an unfounded claim that her occupancy was permissive.
Please treat any earlier letter from me that said the titles merged in 1983 as corrected by this email. The dates that matter are:
1982/83 — first registration of two titles, without the occupier being heard;
24 July 1986 — first-instance judgment describing one farm while two titles still stood;
2 February 1987 — amalgamation, before the appeal ended;
31 July 1987 — Court of Appeal.
Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler
Refs where relevant: N610CGV; 260919-6726246; titles WA231076 and WA240304.
Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your e-mail and for clarifying the subject of your enquiry.

As you know the Manorial Documents Register (MDR) only gives general descriptions of the content, extent and location of the manorial records recorded in the register: LLANDOUGH MANOR | The National Archives<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/c/F236775> The manorial records for the Manor of Llandough are held at the National Library of Wales, Glamorgan Archives and West Glamorgan Archives, and their catalogues can be accessed on-line : NLW Catalogue<https://discover.library.wales/discovery/search?vid=44WHELF_NLW:44WHELF_NLW_NUI> , Glamorgan Archives Catalogue<https://canfod.glamarchives.gov.uk/en/> and Archive Collections - Swansea<https://www.swansea.gov.uk/archivecollections?lang=en>

The Welsh entries in the online MDR were added in the 1990’s were based on the survey returns to the Manorial Documents Committee received from institutions and private owners during the 1920’s. These were subsequently passed to the custody of the Historical Manuscripts Commission in 1959 which amalgamated with the Public Record Office to form The National Archives in 2003. I have requested to see the original returns for Manor of Llandough to see if they can provide any additional information on the documentation relating to the manor (Ref. HMC 9/311: https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C5879336 )

There are several other manors with a similar name in Glamorgan and a MDR search using the search term “Llandough” gives the following result: Search results: Llandough Glamorgan | The National Archives<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/results/c?_q=Llandough&_sf=text_man&_ocn=Glamorgan&_naet=M&_st=mdrc>   Sometimes the administration of different manors were brought together and this appears to have occurred  with the Llandough and St May’s Church Manors : https://archives.library.wales/index.php/manors-of-llandough-and-st-mary-church

I will contact you again once I have had an opportunity to look at the original returns sent to Manorial Documents Committee. I hope this preliminary information is of assistance.

Yours sincerely

[The National Archives logo]
Philip Gale | Head of the Collections and Cultural Property Team

Twitter: @UkNatArchives
The National Archives, Kew, Richmond, Surrey [postcode redacted]
